To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the collagen of healing corneal tissue is different from that of normal cornea.
corneal scar formation is associated with a change in the collagen content and that this change may be responsible for the failure of healing corneal tissue to produce a normal, functioning cornea.
corneal scars contain a collagen that is more resistant to degradation than is collagen from normal developing rabbit corneas.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the biochemical changes which occur during the healing of corneal wounds in rabbits.
the study of collagen metabolism in normal and scar tissue.
the molecular structure of collagen and the relationship between the collagen structure and the development of the corneoscleral tissue.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

collagen in normal cornea is more soluble than that in corneal scars; the predominant collagen in corneas of all ages was type I; and collagen in healing corneal scars contains an increased proportion of type AB.
the collagen in corneal scars is not the same as that in normal developing cornea.
collagen type AB may play a role in the pathogenesis of corneal scarring.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
corneal collagen is a mixture of types I and AB, with type AB increasing from 6% to 11% of the total corneal collagen as the cornea matures.
collagen type I is a major component of the cornea, while collagen type AB is a minor component.
the scar tissue in the cornea is a result of an abnormal collagen metabolism.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the corneal collagen matrix in healing tissue is different from that in normal cornea.
corneal scar formation is not a normal process, but a pathological one.
corneal scarring, which is the major cause of vision impairment and blindness, may be due to a fundamental change in collagen structure.
